state.constraints: Judge experimental engineering for an agent-authored language with no external users and no need to retain old interfaces. Semantic correctness, declared boundaries and robust agent edits are primary; count all tokens through successful repair as a secondary metric, without optimizing for human comfort or line count. Native JavaScript/Bun/web operations should implement equivalent behavior, supplemented only to preserve Can contracts and immutable data. Your choice is advisory preparation, never a syntax decision or a customer-facing commitment. Use solely the evidence provided rather than assuming researched facts.
state.evidence_status: Treat 02a549d28fd5fc5c3996160e65a97de332390d30 as the inspected implementation revision. Qualification covers bun-1.4.2-darwin-arm64-v1 alone, with Linux still unverified; documented native features must be exercised on pinned binaries. Audits and isolated tests exist, but this evidence does not contain running invoice/webhook flows, an account-search 503 browser reproduction, a Can browser compiler, offline experiments, a schema snapshot validator or measured agent comparisons. Those missing demonstrations limit the strength of advice. Can-written client and server remain the wider goal; SSR and a client in another language are narrower baselines.
state.routes: The DI-09a baseline uses named handlers mounted at literal paths; dynamic segments are disallowed. Tenant/invoice identifiers can instead travel as query text with application parsing, with shared URL helpers or an endpoint record centralizing construction. html::url proves only URL admission, never an endpoint's existence, verb, input shape or live target. Exact-path checked identity can tie declaration and request/response/method/URL consumers together. Capture support expands that work to conversion failures, encode/decode parity, slash handling, invalid escapes and route conflict ordering. Although Bun documents parameter routes, the pinned build has not been tested. Cross-package identity is required, and source identifier refactors are separate from wire-path edits.
state.forms: In DI-09b, shallow string/optional-string/string-array records are the admitted form schema. The decoder enforces UTF-8 and escape validity, rejects unknown fields or duplicate scalar controls, and keeps repeated array values. A separate validation step builds domain records while preserving rejected text and collecting unrelated field failures. Repeated names across columns supply no checked row pairing. Compare an alignment-checked array representation, keyed row paths with validation, and a distinct JSON endpoint under the existing exact codec. Semantics must cover missing/empty/partial rows, repeated keys, reorder/delete and persistent field-error identity. Ordinary form encoding stays distinct from JSON; protected values and server checks cannot be bypassed.
state.actions_html: The existing DI-09d idiom explicitly maps application cases in named response functions. Can's HTMX asset swaps status 422 and suppresses all remaining 4xx/5xx swaps; this implies the 503 account-search body will not appear, but that exact browser experiment has not run. Possible additions are a configured application status policy, checked per-result mappings or scoped target identities. Conditional DOM disappearance is not ruled out by a typed target name. Real HTTP codes 200/422/409/403/503, retained fields, focus/error announcements and ordering of replies all matter. DI-10 already offers immutable safe HTML constructors and factored render helpers using Bun.escapeHTML plus runtime URL, attribute and structural validation. Static literal-call analysis or checked component declarations could move known faults earlier. Retain runtime validation for unknown values, URL constraints and controlled browser assets; admit neither raw HTML nor authored script, and treat accessibility element coverage separately.
state.browser: Can currently authors Bun applications with safe HTML/HTMX only; browser JS/TS supplied by an app is outside admission. Showing SSR or a foreign-language typed client establishes less than the requested Can-written rich frontend. The bounded candidate is a distinct main-thread browser build admitting shared validation/data, DOM/event work, Fetch, explicit local transitions/rendering and lifecycle cleanup. Workers cannot touch the document and require separate treatment. Server environment, SQL, process/file and HTTP operations must neither remain callable through imports/generics/callbacks nor leak into the bundle. Both targets need identical exact integer and finite-float wire behavior, record and tagged variant/option encodings, unknown/duplicate rejection, immutable aliases and boxed completions. Full int behavior cannot be presumed from Number. No such browser build or parity experiment is in the evidence.
state.offline_lifecycle: Three technical offline models await evaluation: live-view memory edits with manual retry; a versioned local draft restored subject to storage availability and explicitly submitted; and a durable mutation queue with stable IDs, ordered recovery/reconciliation and server-supported deduplication. The online flag is merely advisory about connectivity. Local persistence introduces identity isolation across tenants/users, sign-out behavior, schema upgrades and quota/eviction outcomes. Queued effects also introduce multi-tab races, expired authorization and crash recovery. Do not conflate either with offline app-shell reload or background synchronization, and do not make a product promise from the selected trial baseline. Independently, saves require the acknowledged server revision, present draft, identified pending change and outcome state, preserving edits newer than a reply. Listener/timer cleanup and suppression of disposed-view updates are local duties; Fetch abort cannot reverse a server write. View and application owners must distinguish work that ends on disposal from tracked mutations that continue, with uncertain effects reconciled.
state.observation: Existing DI-13 attached tests inspect Can computations and fixture queues, but bare => ok on an opaque server result cannot inspect its protocol contents, resulting DOM or lasting effects. Today's layered alternative uses companion HTTP, browser and live-database observations. Consider improving that tooling, admitting read-only HTTP projections, or introducing a source-authored multi-layer scenario runner. An HTTP-level projection is insufficient to certify target updates. Reusable fixtures must preserve argument checks, isolated FIFO invocation identity and caller-rename stability via DI-06. Observation adequacy is tested by incorrect success bodies, executable hostile output, suppressed 503 rendering, wrong database rows despite a correct UI and duplicate webhook effects behind success statuses. Missing integration runs remain explicitly missing; no scenario machinery supplies universal proof.
state.sql: For DI-14, Can statically checks descriptors and parameter/cardinality admission and dynamically binds parameters and validates row names, scalar types and values. Only bounded SELECT can return rows; mutation execute returns counts and disallows RETURNING. Canonical post-write values currently need a known-value response or a transaction-local follow-up read. PostgreSQL's native RETURNING can be assessed if mutation forms, dialect, finite result bounds, zero rows and row codecs are explicit. It cannot replace tenant/revision protection at the write or stated isolation/locking, since Read Committed does not freeze an earlier read. Nor can it resolve commit_unknown after a commit decision; durable operation identity and reconciliation remain necessary. Schema agreement is not checked at compile time today. The alternatives add migration-backed database tests, a reproducible schema snapshot with version/provenance and staleness/deployment checks, or builds consulting a named live schema. Each still needs runtime row checks and verification that the deployed database matches what was checked.
state.cancellation: DI-15 currently keeps ownership and resource leases for all unsettled participants, including race losers, without automatic cancellation. Deadlines on close/shutdown limit the caller's patience but cannot discard the underlying lease or terminate arbitrary native work; a never-settling owner can hold drain forever. Fetch and stream adapters support particular cancellation actions. Documented SQL reservation abort covers only waiting before acquisition and establishes nothing about cancelling an executing query. Existing native semantics leave an empty Promise.race unresolved and make empty Promise.any fail; explicit nonempty guards are the current idiom. Compare per-operation controls plus qualified supervisor timeout/kill, a context conveyed only to cancellable adapters, and worker/process separation to stop bounded computations at serialization/recovery cost. Keep cancel intent distinct from settlement, actual release and host termination; forced exit is not rollback or cleanup evidence. Probe disconnect around commit/outbox delivery, a hung loser and forced shutdown using owner/lease counts, database state and external effects on a named installed target.
